Architecture

All_Diets.csv
   │
   ├─► data_analysis.py ──► output/  (CSV tables + 3 charts + summary.json)
   │        (Docker container, batch path)
   │
   └─► upload_dataset.py ─► Azurite Blob emulator  (container "datasets")
                                   │
                                   ▼
                        lambda_function.py  (manual invocation)
                                   │
                                   ▼
                    simulated_nosql/results.json  (5 diet documents)

Shared cleaning and aggregation logic lives in diet_core.py, so the batch path and the Blob path produce identical means (verified by scripts/verify_outputs.py).

Speaker script

There are two paths. The batch path reads the CSV and produces tables and charts. The cloud path uploads the CSV to Azurite, and our function downloads it with the Azure Blob SDK, computes per-diet averages and stores them as JSON documents. Both paths share one core module, and a verification script confirms they give the same numbers. The function is invoked manually — Azurite has no event triggers — and we say so openly.

Slide 4 / 11Task 1 · ≈ 60 s

Task 1 — Analysis and cleaning

Cleaning rules

  • Trim and lower-case diet / cuisine labels (“Paleo” = “paleo”)
  • Invalid, negative or missing macros → column mean (0 imputed in this dataset)
  • Ratios with a zero denominator stay blank, never infinity (38 undefined Carbs-to-Fat values)

Outputs

  • Mean macros per diet
  • Top 5 protein recipes per diet (25 rows)
  • Most common cuisine per diet
  • Protein-to-Carbs and Carbs-to-Fat ratios

Speaker script

We normalise labels so the same diet is not split by capitalisation, and we convert macros to numbers, replacing invalid values with the column mean. In this dataset no values actually needed imputing. Ratios divided by zero are left blank instead of infinity — 38 recipes have zero fat. The three charts are a bar chart of averages, a heatmap of diets versus nutrients, and a scatter of the top five protein recipes by cuisine.

Speaker script

Keto wins on average protein per recipe, but only by a hair over Mediterranean. Mediterranean wins on total protein only because it has the most recipes, so we report both and explain the difference. Vegan recipes are the most carbohydrate-heavy. American is the top cuisine for four diets; Mediterranean diet recipes are mostly Mediterranean cuisine. These are recipe-level numbers, not serving sizes.

Speaker script

We containerised the analysis with a multi-stage Dockerfile and used Docker Compose to orchestrate Azurite, the analysis job, the uploader and the function. To practise push and pull workflows without a cloud account, we ran a local registry, pushed the image, pulled it back and ran it successfully.

Task 3 — Serverless function on Azurite

  1. Azurite runs as a Compose service on the Blob endpoint …:10000/devstoreaccount1
  2. upload_dataset.py creates container datasets and uploads All_Diets.csv
  3. lambda_function.py downloads the blob with azure-storage-blob, cleans it, averages macros per diet
  4. Result saved to simulated_nosql/results.json: one document per diet
Processed 7806 recipes from datasets/All_Diets.csv;
stored 5 diet documents in simulated_nosql/results.json

Inside Compose the endpoint host is azurite (not 127.0.0.1); the account key is Microsoft’s public emulator key.

Speaker script

Azurite stands in for Azure Blob Storage. We upload the CSV to a container, then our function downloads it through the real Azure SDK, pointed at the emulator, and writes five JSON documents to a local folder that plays the role of a NoSQL database. Because Azurite has no event triggers, the function is invoked manually — it is a simulation of a serverless function, not an Azure Functions host.

Task 4 — CI/CD with GitHub Actions

  • Workflow stages: build image → pytest (10 tests) → flake8 → start Azurite → run upload + function → compare batch vs. Blob means → local-registry push/pull → run retrieved image
  • GitHub-hosted runners start their own Azurite, because they cannot reach a local VM
  • Optional Docker Hub publishing through DOCKERHUB_USERNAME variable and DOCKERHUB_TOKEN secret

Slide 9 / 11Task 5 · ≈ 75 s

Task 5 — Two enhancements, measured

A. Smaller image (multi-stage build)

698 → 568 MB

−130 MB (−18.6 %). Baseline: full python:3.11 with pip cache. Optimised: slim runtime, venv copied from a builder, no pip cache.

B. Faster data processing

11.0× faster

7,806 rows: 13.72 ms → 1.25 ms (median).
156,120 rows (20× replicated stress test): 90.75 ms → 11.96 ms = 7.6×.

  • Method: one warm-up, 15 measured runs, medians; results checked numerically equal; aggregation only, excluding I/O and cleaning.
  • Size gain comes from dropping the full base image and cache — not from “having two stages” by itself.
  • The 20× workload repeats the same rows; it is a stress test, not new data.

Speaker script

We chose two enhancements. First, a multi-stage build with a slim runtime cut the image from about 698 to 568 megabytes. Second, we optimised the aggregation step and measured it: about eleven times faster on the real dataset and 7.6 times on a twenty-times replicated workload. We used a warm-up, fifteen runs and medians, and we are clear that the benchmark covers only the aggregation step.
